Puppy Crying in Crate? How to Stop Whining Day & Night

Sally Jones5 days ago
198 10 minutes read

If your puppy is crying in the crate, you probably want to know one thing: How do I get them to stop? First, check that your puppy has gone potty, isn’t hungry or uncomfortable, and has had enough activity before crating. Then, use gradual crate training to teach your puppy that the crate is a safe, comfortable place—not a punishment.

The right response also depends on why your puppy is crying. Brief whining may be normal as they adjust, while persistent or frantic crying can signal that they’re scared, uncomfortable, or struggling with being alone. Below, we’ll explain why puppies cry in their crates, how long you should let them cry, and what you can do to help them settle during the day and at night.

Will Your Puppy Ever Like His Crate?

Is your puppy screaming in his crate for hours? With patience and practice, your dog should eventually “cave” in and learn to love his crate. However, it’s best if you ease him into it properly. Dogs are instinctively denning animals, and they find comfort in having a pad of their own.

Puppies cry in crates for many reasons. Often, they are scared, bored, lonely, or anxious. Puppies are not used to being confined to a small space, and they may be confused. Whining and crying are their way of expressing that they are unhappy with the situation.

But first, puppies need assurance that their new crate is a safe, inviting place — not a cage that serves as a long-term babysitter or a tool for punishment (it’s not a time-out chair). Easier said than done, right?

Crate Training Basics

If you take the lead and follow the steps in our crate training article, it can be relatively painless. The earlier you start crate training, the better. This guide walks you through the basics, including recommended crates. If you’ve read that article, tried those tactics, and still have trouble with whining, then read on for some additional tips.

Is This Normal Or A Problem?

Some crying and whining is normal when a puppy is first getting used to a crate, especially during the first few nights. Brief fussing may simply mean your puppy is adjusting to being alone or learning that crate time is part of their routine.

However, persistent or frantic crying shouldn’t be ignored. If your puppy is panicking, trying to escape, hurting themselves, excessively drooling, vomiting, or showing other signs of severe distress, stop and reassess the crate-training approach. Your puppy may need shorter crate sessions, more gradual training, or help from your veterinarian or a qualified dog trainer.

8 Real-Life Scenarios: Your Puppy Won’t Stop Crying In the Crate At Night

Puppies cry in their crates for many reasons, and the cause can change as they adjust to crate training. You don’t have to lose sleep over a crying puppy, so before assuming your puppy is being difficult, consider what’s happening immediately before the crying starts and whether there are other signs of discomfort or distress.

1. Crying the First Night

The first night in a crate can be especially difficult. Your puppy has just left their mother and littermates and is suddenly sleeping alone in an unfamiliar environment. Some whining or crying is normal while they adjust. Keeping the crate near your bed, making it comfortable, and establishing a calm bedtime routine can help your puppy feel more secure.

2. Crying After a Potty Break

Bathroom breaks are critical, especially for puppies whose bladders can’t last long. Make sure your puppy does all his business outside as close to bedtime as possible. Don’t worry — the older your pup gets, the longer he’ll go without needing to go potty.

If your puppy cries after you take them outside to potty, they may simply be awake and ready to play rather than ready to go back to sleep. Keep nighttime potty trips quiet and boring: take your puppy out, give them an opportunity to potty, and return them to the crate without playtime or excitement. If they keep crying, make sure they aren’t still uncomfortable or need another bathroom break.

3. Crying For Hours

Hours of continuous crying can mean your puppy is struggling with the crate or being left alone rather than simply protesting bedtime. Check basic needs such as potty, hunger, temperature, and comfort, then consider whether you moved through crate training too quickly. If your puppy is frantic, attempting to escape, hurting themselves, or showing other signs of severe distress, don’t rely on prolonged “cry it out” as your training strategy.

4. Crying When Left Alone During The Day

If your puppy cries as soon as you leave during the day, they may not yet be comfortable being alone. Start with very short periods apart and gradually increase the time as your puppy learns that you leave and come back. Providing a safe chew or food-filled stimulating toy can also give your puppy something positive to focus on while they’re alone.

5. Barking vs. Whining

Whining is often a puppy’s way of expressing discomfort, uncertainty, frustration, or a desire for attention. Barking can have similar causes, but repeated or escalating barking may indicate that your puppy is becoming increasingly frustrated or distressed. Pay attention to your puppy’s body language and the situation, not just the sound they’re making.

6. Your Puppy Has Too Much Energy

A puppy who hasn’t had enough age-appropriate exercise, play, training, or mental stimulation may have a hard time settling down in a crate. Before crating, give your puppy an opportunity to use the bathroom and engage in appropriate activity. The goal isn’t to exhaust your puppy, but to meet their needs so they’re more prepared to relax. It can also help to take your dog on a long walk and play with him before bed to burn off that energy.

7. Suddenly Crying After Doing Fine

A puppy that was previously comfortable in their crate but suddenly starts crying deserves a little extra attention. A change in routine, a frightening experience, needing to potty more often, or physical discomfort could be responsible. If the change is sudden or your puppy also shows symptoms such as vomiting, diarrhea, lethargy, pain, or changes in appetite, contact your veterinarian to rule out an underlying health problem.

8. The Crate Is Too Much, Too Fast

Sometimes the problem isn’t the crate itself but the pace of training. If your puppy regularly cries as soon as the crate door closes, you may be asking for more than they’re ready to handle. Go back to shorter, easier sessions, reward calm behavior, and gradually increase the duration.

How To Get A Puppy Used To A Crate

If your puppy cries in his crate before bed (or anytime):

  • Make sure you place good bedding and a few favorite toys in the crate.
  • Also consider the room temperature. Puppies and smaller dog breeds can get chilly quickly, so place the crate in an area that’s not too cold (or too hot).
  • If the crate is too large, your dog could feel intimidated, so choose the best crate for your dog’s size.

If you’ve done all you can to meet your pup’s basic needs, consider putting him to bed with a chewable treat or super-strong toy. This will distract your puppy and hopefully wear him out until he nods off.

Why Is Your Puppy Still Whining? What To Check First

If your puppy is still whining after you’ve started crate training, don’t assume they’re simply trying to get your attention. First, check their basic needs and consider whether the crate experience is moving faster than your puppy can comfortably handle. Here’s what to check first:

  • Potty: Young puppies have small bladders and may genuinely need to go, particularly overnight. If it has been a while since their last potty break, take them out calmly and give them a chance to relieve themselves.
  • Hunger or thirst: Make sure your puppy has been fed appropriately and has access to fresh water. Follow your veterinarian’s guidance about feeding and water schedules, particularly around bedtime.
  • Temperature: Check that your puppy isn’t too hot, cold, or exposed to a draft.
  • Crate size: Your puppy should have enough room to stand up, turn around, lie down, and stretch comfortably without too much extra space.
  • Bedding: Make sure the bedding is comfortable, clean, and safe for your puppy. Some puppies may prefer less bedding, especially if they chew or become overheated.
  • Fear or overstimulation: An overtired, frightened, or overwhelmed puppy may have trouble settling. Try lowering the noise and activity around the crate and giving your puppy time to calm down.

Give Your Puppy Time To Adjust

Once your puppy’s needs are met, avoid immediately letting them out every time they whine. Otherwise, your puppy may learn that crying consistently ends the crate session. When possible, wait for a brief moment of quiet before opening the crate or offering attention.

However, this doesn’t mean you should leave a distressed puppy to cry indefinitely. There’s an important difference between a puppy who fusses briefly because they would rather be out playing and one who is becoming increasingly frantic or frightened. If your puppy is panicking, trying to escape, hurting themselves, or unable to settle, take a step back and make crate training more gradual.

Try shorter crate sessions and reward your puppy for entering the crate and remaining calm. Gradually increase the time they spend inside as they become more comfortable. The goal isn’t simply to get your puppy to stop making noise—it’s to help them learn that the crate is a safe, predictable place to relax.

Crate time can help puppies develop confidence and independence when introduced positively and used appropriately. Just be careful not to overuse the crate or use it as punishment. If your puppy consistently becomes extremely distressed when separated from you, talk with your veterinarian or a qualified dog behavior professional for guidance.

How Long To Let Your Puppy Cry In His Crate

If you do have to crate your puppy more than you’d like (long workday, tons of errands to run, etc.), make sure you spend extra time playing with him or taking him on walks in between crate times. And don’t forget that a puppy’s bladder can’t go for long periods of time without relief — no more than a few hours at a time at first.

Important Note

According to the Animal Humane Society , leaving a puppy in a crate for an 8-10 hour workday is “not an appropriate way” to crate train. If you have times when you can’t be there, ask a neighbor or hire a pet sitter to give your pup a break. The more attention they have while outside of the crate, the less time they spend whining and crying once back in the crate.

What If My Puppy Won’t Stop Barking In His Crate?

If your puppy is still crying at night after 3 weeks or so, try placing a blanket over his crate for comfort. You might also have bigger issues beyond crate training itself. Dogs need to know that you’re in charge. If they don’t trust you, they won’t behave well no matter how hard you try. Once your puppy earns your respect, then he’ll realize that you’re putting him in his crate for his own good.

And remember, resist all temptation to go to the crate. If you acknowledge your puppy’s whining with attention, he’ll learn that all he has to do is cry, and you’ll be there. As challenging as it might be, let your dog settle himself down. After a few nights, he should understand that whining and crying in the crate won’t get him anywhere. Get some earplugs (or use a white noise app on your phone) and know it’s a short-term sacrifice for long-term happiness for you and your pup.

Personal Experience With My Puppy Crying In The Crate

My Poogle (Poodle Beagle Mix) Falkor is about two and a half years old. I crate-trained him from day one, but it was not an easy or quiet process. He was particularly unhappy being left in the crate when no one was home. We have a big house, with multiple floors, as well as other animals. It is not safe to leave him out at night, or when we are gone, so crate-training was a must.

It took almost 3 months to get Falkor to quiet down in his crate during puppy training. Even now, he still whines and cries if we are leaving or if he doesn’t want to be in the crate. However, if he whines and cries when we are home, he has to stay in his crate longer until he pipes down. While the major temper tantrums and crying are no longer happening, I still do not give in to any whining, as I know it will undo all the hard work we have done to get him comfortable in the crate.

–Danielle DeGroot, Poogle parent

Frequently Asked Questions

As a pet owner, questions can sometimes feel endless. Let the questions and answers below help you out, and for any more questions or concerns, write to us in the comments.

Should I Let My Puppy Cry In The Crate At Night?

Brief whining can be part of normal crate adjustment, but you shouldn’t assume every cry should be ignored. First, consider whether your puppy needs to potty or is genuinely distressed; if their basic needs are met, give them a chance to settle while gradually building their comfort with the crate.

Should You Close A Puppy Crate At Night?

You should keep the crate door closed at night for at least the first few months. This will eliminate any confusion and ensure your puppy doesn’t try to sneak out, especially when you’re asleep. Even if your puppy is crying in the crate at night, keep the door closed until you have fully crate-trained him. It may be loud, but you must establish this boundary now while he is young.

When Should You Move The Puppy Crate Out Of Your Bedroom?

When your puppy stops whining in his crate, you can slowly start to transition him to another room. Start by moving the crate closer to the door. Then, eventually, move it to its permanent place in the home.

Remember Why You’re Doing The Tough Training

It’s not easy housebreaking puppies — remember, they’re in a new place, away from their mom and litter. When you’re working on getting your puppy to stop crying in his crate, remember that this is an all-new environment, and your puppy needs time and reassurance to adjust.

As time-consuming and frustrating as crate training (and other puppy behavior problems) might be at first, your hard work will surely pay off in the long run. And if you still find yourself struggling, you might look into professional training (especially while your dog is young). We recommend an online dog training program like Doggy Dan’s online course or a local dog trainer.

Remember: keep your eye on the prize. Your end goal is for your puppy to want to be in his crate.

    Nicole
    November 25, 2019 5:24 am

    I have always used crates. While the first month or so can be hard, once they get used to the crate it can benefit them more than you. When I trained my pups (between 6 weeks and 3 months when they came to live with me) I did 2 important things. One is that often I would put them in the crate close but not latch the door. Sometimes I would leave the room others stay in the room. I taught them it was their “safe space”. Sometimes they would get nervous around guests or other dogs and would walk right into the crate. I would leave the crate door open and they came out when they felt better. I still socialized them, but often they just wanted a break.

    One of my dogs is particularly skiddish. If it thundered she would beg to go into her crate of the door to the room was closed. There were still times that they cried to get out. I just laid on the floor, kept them in the crate but calmed them down. Toys in the crate are particularly important. My dog is now 7 and I can’t remember the last time we closed the door on the crate but she probably goes in there and takes a nap at least once a day. And if there is bad thunder, she goes right in. She is now allowed on our bed and has complete house access when we leave. But if we leave the house, there is a 90% chance she will just be in her crate asleep and calmly walk right to the door to wait to go outside.
    I’ve never thought of it as a convenience for me or a punishment. It is the only place in the house or yard that is ‘hers’ and she knows she will be safe. We recently adopted a new puppy and do have to crate him when we leave – he is a scavenger and might get into something dangerous. But the adult goes in, lays next to his crate and he is fine.
    Just a few ideas for people that are struggling….

    Ashley
    Reply to  Millie
    October 27, 2019 9:51 pm

    Are you crating him during the day even when you guys are home? Putting a puppy in it’s crate ONLY at night is a bad habit when trying to crate train. He will associate that with you leaving him at night which could cause separation issues. It’s best to crate him multiple times throughout the day when you are home so he doesn’t associate the crate with you leaving him in it only at night. Always put toys or treats in there with him. Of course, proper exercise and potty breaks are a must. Every puppy is different but he will get properly crate trained!

    So I went through two different crates and two beds to get this right. I use crate at night and when hes sleeping during the day. Bought smaller crate and trained on grass puppy pads, crate moved to bedroom and moved away from regular puppy pads. Potty use been correct all day for first time and had treats and toys on the new bed in his new crate all day with the door open. Treat and praise everytime he walked in there by choice. Then ignored cries completely, waited for a long pause – I was ready and waiting for it so be ready to quickly walk over. Grabbed a comfy blanket-like pyjama top of mine (worn not washed) and wrapped this loosely around him with a good stroke and a good boy. Not a peep since. First time in 2 weeks.     Correct the dog!!!! Tap top of crate with a firm no. All the dog knows is, if he whines he gets let out.
